At an effective spatial resolution of $0.052'' \times 0.042''$ ($7.8 \times 6.3$ au), the image reveals a bright main ring at radii of $\sim20$--$70$ au and an unresolved compact emission component tracing the inner disk around the central star. Ellipse fits centered on the stellar position to contours tracing the inner and outer edges of the ring reveal radial variations in position angles and inclinations. At the inner edge ($\sim21$--$26$ au), the position angle and inclination span $214^\circ$--$233^\circ$ and $23^\circ$--$39^\circ$, respectively, while they span $231^\circ$--$235^\circ$ and $33^\circ$--$36^\circ$ at the outer edge ($\sim58$--$67$ au). Whereas a coplanar ring toy model fails to reproduce such variations, a warped ring model with the local tilt decreasing from $\sim4^\circ$ at $r = 20$ au to $\sim1^\circ$ at 60 au reproduces them. The high-pass-filtered real-part image reveals a pair of opposed curved negative residuals. Similar features appear only in the warped ring model, further supporting the dust warp. These results establish CQ Tau as an example of a warped dust disk and an important laboratory for investigating the connection between three-dimensional disk geometry and planet formation.

papers.title: Post-DART impact ejecta re-accumulation on Dimorphos and implications for Hera gravity measurements
papers.abstract: Context. The DART impact might have substantially modified the surface and near-surface structure of Dimorphos, affecting the morphology and gravity field that is to be measured by ESA's Hera mission. Aims. We investigate the post-impact redistribution of ejecta and its dependence on the assumed internal structure of Dimorphos. Methods. We performed high-resolution SPH simulations of the DART impact into two low-cohesion rubble-pile models, with and without a large central boulder. We followed the processes of ejecta re-accumulation and gravity evolution for six hours. Results. The impact ejects about 13% of Dimorphos's mass, most of which is re-accreted, producing near-global resurfacing. The ejecta blanket exceeds 8 m around the impact depression but is only a few tens of centimetres thick near the antipode, with similar large-scale deposition in both interior models. Local gravity changes reach about 10% of the pre-impact value. The central boulder affects the surface gravity only within the impact depression, where the removal of overlying material enhances its gravitational contribution. Conclusions. Hera will observe a surface and gravity field substantially modified by DART, which must be considered when interpreting measurements in terms of the internal structure of Dimorphos.

papers.title: Lunar tidal response-induced clock frequency variations on the Moon
papers.abstract: As clock performance improves, the instability and uncertainty of the clock's fractional frequency shift (FFS) become comparable to the FFS caused by the lunar tidal response (LTR), so the influence of the LTR on lunar time needs to be investigated. In this paper, we used the Keplerian expansions method to study the FFS to the level of $10^{-18}$ caused by the LTR between two clocks placed in different positions on the Moon. We consider the case of the Moon orbiting in an elliptical orbit, which is closer to the actual situation compared to the case of the Moon moving in a circular orbit. An interesting phenomenon is found that the longitude difference between two clocks can cause a change in the amplitude and phase of the FFS due to the LTR, but the latitude difference only changes the amplitude of the FFS. We further estimated the clock difference between two clocks near the Moon caused by the LTR. When one clock is on the lunar surface, and the other is on the Earth's surface, the LTR will cause a clock difference of $% -5.68\times 10^{-7}$ $\mu $s/day between the two clocks. These are significant for the construction of a lunar time and clock synchronization near the Moon.

papers.title: Accurate pulsar timing array likelihoods: better low-rank covariance for gravitational wave background
papers.abstract: In pulsar timing array analyses, the stochastic process describing the gravitational wave background is typically modeled using a Fourier basis at discrete frequencies with an interval $\sim 0.1~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, with a diagonal Fourier-domain covariance determined by the power spectral density at the corresponding frequencies. Although this rank-reduced modeling significantly accelerates likelihood evaluation and provides a good approximation in many scenarios, it can lead to biased parameter inference because it is insensitive to spectral features on scales smaller than $\sim 0.1~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. We introduce a better construction of the low-rank covariance for low-frequency processes by maximizing the log-likelihood averaged over an ensemble of realizations drawn from the true model likelihood. In this approach, the basis-domain covariance matrix is sensitive to the entire model spectrum and is generally non-diagonal. Using two mock datasets, we demonstrate improved likelihood accuracy and more faithful recovery of spectral features compared to the conventional Fourier-diagonal model. Benchmark tests show that this new model requires a computational cost comparable to that of the conventional approach.

papers.title: Development of an FPGA-Based Readout System and Functional Characterization of a Custom NSX1 ASIC for X-ray instrumentation
papers.abstract: We developed an FPGA-based readout system for a front-end ASIC (NSX1) with 64 channels to read out a large- area silicon drift detector used in X-ray detection instruments such as the Wide Field Monitor module for the STROBE-X mission concept. The FPGA acts as a central controller for the NSX1 configuration, implementing trigger handling and event sequencing, precise event timestamping, control of an external ADC for digitization, and data transfer to the host PC. The system enables comprehensive ASIC characterization; here, we demonstrate preliminary ASIC functionality and characterization tests using a calibrated pulser for two programmable linear gain responses of 375 mV/fC and 750 mV/fC. These preliminary results validate the low-noise performance of the NSX1 ASIC and demonstrate successful integration of the DAQ system.

papers.title: FastPM: Fast Pretrained Model for Cosmological Simulation-Based Inference
papers.abstract: Modern cosmology increasingly relies on large ensembles of expensive simulations to model the non-linear Universe and extract information from upcoming surveys. However, generating high-fidelity simulations---whether gravity-only N-body or full hydrodynamical---requires substantial computational resources. In this work, we demonstrate that transfer learning from fast low-fidelity simulations can dramatically reduce the cost of training machine learning models, in particular for simulation-based inference (SBI). We train a Fast Pretrained Model (FastPM) on a set of Fast Particle-Mesh (FastPM) simulations to infer $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$ from the power spectrum, and finetune on a smaller set of high-fidelity CAMELS N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. To reach a fixed posterior accuracy, the pretrained model requires only 5--15\% of the high-fidelity simulations compared to the number of simulations needed when training on CAMELS alone, reducing the total training simulation compute cost, including that of the pretraining simulations, by up to an order of magnitude in CPU hours. Remarkably, the gains persist for the total matter power spectrum of full hydrodynamical simulations: although FastPM contains no baryonic physics, pretraining on FastPM runs that together cost less than a single hydrodynamical simulation still reduces the total training simulation compute by a factor of $\sim$5. Moreover, pretraining on more accurate FastPM runs yields more accurate posteriors than training on CAMELS alone achieves with any number of simulations we consider. These results demonstrate that transfer learning from fast simulations is a simple and powerful route to high-fidelity SBI, and highlight the promise of simulation-based foundation models in cosmology.

papers.title: Near-exact Upper Confidence Limits for Axion Haloscopes
papers.abstract: The data acquisition of axion haloscopes commonly implements sequential adaptive frequency scans. We present a method to calculate likelihood-based upper confidence limits on axion-photon coupling under this circumstance. We compare the likelihood-based method conceptually and quantitatively with tailor-made methods, i.e. the one proposed by Brubaker et al. (Geometric) and its upgrade the Bayesian Power-Measured (BPM) framework proposed by Palken et al. We find that the likelihood method yields average upper limits that are significantly more constraining than those obtained from these methods. For example, expected constraints improve by a factor of 1.4 as compared with the current state of the art when applied to projections for the ALPHA Plasma-haloscope. We further clarify the statistical basis for the Geometric and BPM methods. In particular, we point out the correspondence of BPM to e-values, proposed as an alternative to conventional p-values in statistics.

papers.title: ePNGCAT: the first eROSITA all-sky data release
papers.abstract: The eROSITA telescope array aboard the joint German--Russian Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission delivered the deepest soft all-sky X-ray survey to date, scanning the entire sky more than four times between December 2019 and February 2022. The potential of the survey remains, however, hampered by the fact that only data for the half of the sky owned by the German consortium have been released publicly, whereas the other half remains accessible only to the Russian consortium, effectively making eROSITA a "half-sky" survey for most applications. The only publicly accessible all-sky "data product" as of 2026 is a single press-release image published in June 2020 jointly by both consortia to celebrate the completion of the first all-sky survey (eRASS1). Here I present the first all-sky eROSITA catalogue based on this image, containing around 63 thousand sources with an estimated completeness of about 50% above $3\times10^{-13}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ in the 0.2-2.3 keV band and a positional accuracy of $\sim$1 arcmin, validated against the full eRASS1 catalogue for half the sky and against several external catalogues. The catalogue is thus comparable with 2RXS, the deepest truly all-sky survey generally available, and gives a first glimpse of the eastern Galactic hemisphere with eROSITA. In this hemisphere, about 11000 detected sources have no counterpart in ROSAT or other public X-ray catalogues and are expected to be genuine new X-ray sources. Besides the catalogue, I release calibrated HEALPix maps to facilitate studies of large-scale extended emission, such as the eROSITA bubbles, or of Galactic absorption that require full sky coverage (https://zenodo.org/records/23640281), as well as the complete analysis pipeline to make the results fully reproducible (https://github.com/doroshv/eropngcat).

papers.title: Magnetic Topological Evolution and the Predictive Role of Winding-flux-based Masked PILs in Extreme Solar Flares from AR13664 and AR13842
papers.abstract: Using vector magnetogram data from the Helioseismic Magnetic Imager (HMI) on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), we present detailed case studies of precursor activity in Active Regions (ARs) 13664 and 13842, which produced several intense flares. We examined the spatiotemporal evolution of key magnetic topological parameters, including winding, helicity, winding-flux-based masked polarity inversion lines (PILs), and PIL gradients, from the precursor to the post-flare phases. The temporal evolution of the winding flux showed a significant enhancement during the precursor phase, and this trend was consistent across the seven X-class and five M-class flares (>= M5.0). The spatial distribution of both raw and Gaussian-smoothed winding-flux enhancement is co-located with flare footpoint regions of highly twisted core fields, as indicated by the photospheric magnetic topology. The winding-flux-based masked PILs that persisted around the flare locations showed a significant increase in strength and area during the precursor activity. These masked PILs spatially coincide with regions likely hosting non-potential core magnetic fields associated with the observed flares. Furthermore, the gradient of strong PILs extracted from the ARs was positively correlated with flare-associated locations and typically increased several hours (approx. 3-5 h) before flare onset. By imposing a gradient threshold on strong PILs, we isolate magnetic regions repeatedly associated with flare initiation, providing useful constraints in regimes where current flare-forecasting models remain uncertain. Therefore, the combined analysis of the spatiotemporal evolution of different magnetic topological parameters enhances our understanding of intense solar flare forecasting and the identification of potential triggering sites, thereby contributing to improved space weather prediction frameworks.

papers.title: LunarRF: A Terrain-Aware Propagation Engine and Pole-Wide 3GPP Surface Coverage Atlas of the Lunar South Pole
papers.abstract: Artemis surface operations will depend on 3GPP cellular links, yet no public product shows where such links are physically possible across the lunar south pole. We present LunarRF, a GPU system for terrain-aware surface coverage, and the pole-wide atlas produced with it. A footprint engine casts 8192 radial profiles from one of 11,827 candidate masts enumerated by stated rules on the orbit-adjusted LOLA elevation model, takes the viewshed, and evaluates ITU-R P.1812 Delta-Bullington propagation on every profile, continuous through the radio horizon. An order-independent resolver merges the footprints per 20 m cell, making the run shardable and resumable. The atlas covers the disc south of 80{\deg}S at 20 m for four SFCG-recommended surface bands and the IM-2 demonstration band, 1.8 to 25.375 GHz, under a stated link budget, storing per cell the best-server power and identity, redundancy count, line of sight and coverability. The engine is validated against a parabolic-equation solver, ray tracing and analytic solutions. Swapping Deygout for Delta-Bullington, or adding terrain noise at the level of the published height-error map of the DEM, moves the coverable class on under 1% of a mast's disc in the mean. With every candidate active, 90.5% of the disc is coverable at 1.8 GHz, 59% at 5.855 GHz and 10% at 25.375 GHz, or 84, 43 and 5% after the measured 3-4 dB engine optimism. A mast covers about 90% of its visible area within its budget-set range, and no band is terrain-limited. The nine current Artemis regions are 85-99% coverable at 1.8 GHz and 22-85% at 5.855 GHz. The atlas and candidate table are released with a DOI.

papers.title: Machine Learning Applications in the Solar Interior and Atmosphere
papers.abstract: The solar interior and atmosphere constitute a strongly coupled, multiscale dynamical system defined by continuous temporal evolution. Predicting the state of this system requires modeling physical interactions that span disparate spatial and temporal scales, constrained by heterogeneous and sparse data. This chapter formalizes the Sun within the mathematical framework of dynamical systems theory, defining a global state vector ($\vec{S}$) governed by thermodynamical, kinetic, and magnetic properties. Because solar observations represent projected, multi-modal, and partially observable measurements ($\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$) of this hidden state, pure physics-based deduction is fundamentally constrained. We present a unifying thesis: the primary role of machine learning in heliophysics is to act as a structured family of mathematical operators---specifically Inference ($\mathcal{I}$), Emulation ($\mathcal{E}$), Propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and Control ($\mathcal{C}$)---that reconstruct, simulate, and couple this global state vector across disparate physical layers. By framing the vast, multi-disciplinary literature within this unified state-space taxonomy, we demonstrate how data-driven techniques bridge observational gaps to resolve hidden multiscale couplings and dramatically accelerate the simulation of non-linear processes, establishing a rigorous pathway to predict the global evolution of the Sun.

papers.title: A frequency-resolved measurement of the scattering law in FRB 20210415C
papers.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) show diverse temporal morphologies, shaped both by their intrinsic emission and by propagation effects such as residual dispersion and multipath scattering. Because several of these effects can broaden a burst asymmetrically, an asymmetric profile does not by itself establish multipath scattering. We measure the frequency dependence of the temporal tail in FRB 20210415C, a bright burst from the repeating source FRB 20210219C. The burst is detected across approximately 400-800 MHz. Frequency-resolved fits yield an empirical exponential-tail timescale, $\tau_{\rm emp}$, that follows $\tau_{\rm emp}\propto\nu^{\alpha}$. Two complementary treatments of the underlying pulse width give $\alpha=-3.95\pm0.07$ and $-4.14\pm0.08$. Both results are consistent with the commonly adopted $\nu^{-4}$ scattering law. The inferred scattering time is approximately 8.0 ms at 583 MHz, exceeding Galactic foreground estimates by a factor of at least $4\times10^{2}$. This favours a dominant contribution beyond the Milky Way, although the data do not localise the scattering screen. FRB 20210415C therefore provides a direct measurement of a scattering law commonly imposed in catalogue analyses.

papers.title: Power spectrum of longitudinal-velocity residuals in the Galactic disk from Gaia DR3 red-giant-branch stars
papers.abstract: Non-axisymmetric structures in the Galaxy produce coherent stellar motions in the Galactic disk. These motions are usually interpreted by assuming parameterized gravitational potentials or specific perturbation models, thereby entangling direct kinematic information with model-dependent assumptions. Using Gaia DR3 astrometry, we analyze the Galactic longitudinal-velocity residuals of nearly four million red-giant-branch stars over $-4 < X_h < 4\, \mathrm{kpc}$ and $-6 < Y_h < 6\, \mathrm{kpc}$ in the heliocentric region. We construct an empirical axisymmetric baseline without introducing any dynamical model, and compute the power spectrum of the residual velocity field. The spectrum exhibits a broad peak at spatial frequency of $f \simeq 0.12 - 0.22\, \mathrm{kpc}^{-1}$, corresponding to a scale of around $5-8\, \mathrm{kpc}$. The residual amplitude is sensitive to the adopted distance scale: inverse-parallax distances $d_\varpi$ yield a peak of around $16\, \mathrm{km\, s^{-1}}$, while the Bailer-Jones geometric distances $r_{\mathrm{geo}}$ yield around $12\, \mathrm{km\, s^{-1}}$. Minimizing the low-frequency power favors a solar radial motion of $U_\odot=10.8\, \mathrm{km\, s^{-1}}$ based on $d_\varpi$ and $U_\odot=10.4\, \mathrm{km\, s^{-1}}$ based on $r_{\mathrm{geo}}$. Collectively, the resulting spectrum establishes Gaia astrometry as a direct probe of disk-wide non-axisymmetric kinematics and provides quantitative targets for future dynamical modeling and interpretation.

papers.title: Calibration requirements for Epoch of Reionization 21-cm signal observations - V. Bias and variance in the cylindrical power spectrum from uGMRT Band 3 observations of the ELAIS-N1 field
papers.abstract: Detection of the redshifted 21-cm signal from neutral hydrogen requires precise control of systematic effects arising from instrumental calibration. In this work, we investigate the impact of both time- and frequency-dependent residual gain and bandpass errors on the estimation of the multifrequency angular power spectrum (MAPS) using radio interferometric observations. We discuss our previously developed analytical framework for estimating bias and excess variance in 21-cm signal MAPS in the presence of these residual errors and apply it to uGMRT Band-3 observations. The statistical properties of the residual gains are derived from the data themselves, including their temporal and spectral correlations. We introduce a robust technique for additionally flagging poor-quality data. Our results show that the excess variance induced by residual gain and bandpass errors dominates over the bias across the range of angular multipoles considered. The amplitude of this variance is comparable to the expected power spectrum upper limit at redshift $z \sim 2.2$, indicating that residual calibration errors can significantly affect the detectability of the 21-cm signal. We further transform the estimated MAPS into ($k_{\perp}, k_{ll}$) space and find the expected foreground wedge structure. Importantly, we observe a significant power leakage into the nominal EoR window, which we attribute to residual calibration systematics. This highlights that even after standard foreground mitigation, time- and frequency-correlated gain errors can introduce mode-mixing and contaminate the EoR window. Our results emphasise the necessity of improved calibration accuracy and robust characterisation of residual gain statistics for current and upcoming interferometric experiments such as the uGMRT and SKA, to enable reliable detection of the cosmological 21-cm signal.

papers.title: SoFTg: A hybrid segmentation framework for solar granulation revealing turbulent convection statistics at DKIST scales
papers.abstract: In this work, we present Solar Feature Tracking: granules (SoFTg), a new hybrid algorithm within the SoFT library designed for the segmentation and tracking of solar granulation. By combining a heuristic approach based on a custom adaptive-thresholding technique with the speed and robustness of deep-learning methods, SoFTg provides a fast, reliable and user-friendly solution for granule segmentation, followed by the standard SoFT approach for tracking. We present a comprehensive evaluation of the algorithm's performance using multiple metrics and analyse the different stages of the processing pipeline. The method is tested on three datasets acquired with the Visible Broadband Imager operating in the red continuum at the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope in Maui, Hawaii. We present distributions of both the lifetime and equivalent diameter of the thousands of granules tracked, providing, for the first time, statistically robust evidence of turbulent convection at the spatial scales now accessible through the high-resolution imaging capabilities of DKIST.

papers.title: The design and flight of the Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations (PUEO)
papers.abstract: Sources of cosmic rays at ultrahigh energies (UHE, $\gtrsim$ 1 EeV) are anticipated to give rise to neutrinos at similar energies by production via propagation interactions either within the source region or on cosmological scales. Measurements of the neutrino flux, flavor, and energy provide significant insight into those underlying processes governing UHE cosmic ray acceleration and propagation. Detecting neutrinos at these energies requires immense detector volumes due to their low predicted flux. We present the balloon-borne mission PUEO (Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations) which is an antenna array designed to detect the Askaryan emission from UHE neutrino interactions in the Antarctic ice. This paper reports on the design considerations and implementations for constructing PUEO, from the design parameters to the as-built validations.

papers.title: Triple Decomposition of Field Gradient Tensors in Space Plasmas
papers.abstract: Characterizing local topology in magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence is fundamental to understanding energy dissipation, intermittency, and coherent structures in space plasmas. Classical double decomposition of velocity ($A_{ij}$) and magnetic ($Z_{ij}$) field gradient tensors into symmetric strain and anti-symmetric rotation components conflates rigid-body rotation with planar sliding shear. Here, we extend the real-Schur-based Triple Decomposition framework to MHD flows, rigorously isolating irrotational normal strain ($N, M$), residual pure shear ($H, K$), and true rigid-body rotation ($R, B$). Applying this method to high-resolution NASA-MMS multi-spacecraft observations in the solar wind and Earth's magnetosheath reveals distinct topological signatures. Solar wind dynamics are predominantly strain-dominated due to spherical radial expansion, whereas magnetosheath turbulence is overwhelmingly shear-dominated, driven by boundary interactions. Crucially, cross-term contributions ($2RH$ and $2KB$) are suppressed to $\le 7\%$ across both plasma regimes, contrasting sharply with neutral fluid turbulence ($\sim 13\%$). This suppression is driven by background magnetic-field-induced anisotropy ($k_\perp \gg k_\parallel$), which confines shearing motions perpendicular to the primary rotation axes. By cleanly separating genuine vortex cores from current sheets and shear layers, the Triple Decomposition provides an objective framework for characterizing plasma turbulence and analyzing data from future multi-spacecraft missions.

papers.title: Core-Collapse Supernovae from Single and Binary-Stripped Massive Stars - I. Explodability and Nucleosynthesis
papers.abstract: Binary interaction can substantially alter massive-star evolution and pre-supernova structure, changing core-collapse outcomes and nucleosynthetic yields. We compare explodability and nucleosynthesis in 66 non-rotating, solar-metallicity single-star and binary-stripped progenitors spanning zero-age main-sequence (ZAMS) masses of $11$-$45\,{\rm M}_\odot$, using the spherically symmetric PUSH framework and nucleosynthesis post-processing. Both populations explode up to $22\,{\rm M}_\odot$, with binary stripping altering explodability at higher ZAMS masses. Successful explosions span similar energies ($\sim$0.4-1.3$\,$B) and remnant masses ($\sim$1.4-2.0$\,{\rm M}_\odot$). The largest nucleosynthetic differences occur at low ZAMS masses, particularly for material undergoing explosive O and Si burning. The $^{56}$Ni yields and iron-group abundances broadly agree with observations of core-collapse supernovae and the metal-poor star HD 84937. When compared with calculations using time-dependent mixing-length theory and a two-parameter explodability criterion for the same progenitors, our results reveal substantial differences in explodability, with agreement on successful explosions for only 5 cases across all three approaches. Nevertheless, elemental yield patterns can remain broadly similar for models that explode successfully across treatments. Salpeter initial-mass-function-weighted yields of most elements differ by $\sim$20% between populations, with K enhanced by a factor of $\sim$3.4 in the binary-stripped population, driven by increased production in the lowest-mass progenitors. Binary-stripped models show closer agreement with empirical core-collapse S, K, and Ca abundance ratios relative to Mg inferred from APOGEE, while Na remains overproduced in both populations. Together, our results highlight the need to account for binarity when interpreting supernova abundance patterns.

papers.title: Contributions of massive stars and classical novae to Galactic 26Al
papers.abstract: The radioactive isotope 26Al is believed to be mainly produced by massive stars and ejected into the interstellar medium through their winds and supernovae. Due to its lifetime of 1.04 Myr, it traces recent nucleosynthesis and star formation. 60Fe is a similarly long-lived (lifetime 3.8 Myr) isotope, and only originating in ccSNe. Stellar evolution models in combination with Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) models tend to over-predict the 60Fe/26Al ratio. Population synthesis models that attempt to explain both, the 26Al mass in the Galaxy and its spatial distribution, only match the observational constraints with an enhanced star formation rate (SFR) of >5 Msun/yr. Classical novae may contribute to the 26Al production, potentially lowering the SFR inferred from massive stars and alleviating tension in the 60Fe/26Al ratio. However, previous studies suggest their contribution is negligible or < 10%. In this work we aim to determine the mass distribution of 26Al as a function of Galactocentric radius and estimate the contribution of (very) massive stars and classical novae to the 1.8 MeV signal. We are using 20 yr of INTEGRAL/SPI observations of the gamma-ray line at 1.8 MeV to test different assumptions on the radial structure of 26Al and compare the resulting mass distribution to different GCE models. For our baseline analysis, all tested source models prefer substantial nova contributions, with best-fit fractions of 77-84%. This alleviates tension in the 60Fe/26Al ratio and lowers the SFR from 26Al measurements accordingly to 1-2 Msun/yr. While it is difficult to gauge both contributions directly, next generation MeV telescopes can potentially identify individual massive stars, such as Gamma-2-Velorum.

papers.title: Binary Progenitors of Electron-capture Supernovae
papers.abstract: Electron-capture supernovae (ECSNe) arise from a narrow progenitor parameter space between oxygen-neon white dwarf formation and iron-core collapse supernovae, governed by the competition between core growth and envelope removal. Binary interactions modify this balance through mass transfer and mergers. Using the binary population synthesis framework POSYDON, we model ECSN progenitors across metallicities from $Z/Z_\odot=2$ to $10^{-4}$, focusing on the initial parameter space, pre-supernova stripping, envelope-based classification, surviving companions, post-supernova orbits, and cosmic event rates. The lower edge of the binary ECSN initial primary mass lies near $7\,M_\odot$, owing to efficient convective overshooting in the POSYDON grids, whereas the upper edge increases with metallicity because stronger line-driven winds require larger initial masses to build carbon-oxygen cores within the ECSN range. Stable mass transfer and mergers occupy distinct regions in initial mass ratio and orbital period space. ECSNe in bound binaries are divided into hydrogen-rich Type II ($\sim30\%$), IIb ($\sim10\%$), and Ib ($\sim60\%$) outcomes according to residual hydrogen and helium envelopes. Across all channels, approximately one-third of ECSNe have a bound companion at explosion; the remaining two-thirds do not. Among these bound systems, approximately $90\%$ of the companions are main-sequence stars at explosion. These companions exhibit a bimodal spin distribution, including a rapidly rotating component associated with prior mass transfer. Evolved-star and compact-object companions each account for only a few percent. Combining the formation efficiencies with cosmic star formation and metallicity evolution models yields an intrinsic ECSN rate peaking at $z\sim2-3$ and declining at higher redshifts. Over cosmic history, ECSNe contribute approximately $1\%-4\%$ of all core-collapse supernovae.

papers.title: Revisiting supernova constraints on dark gauge bosons
papers.abstract: We revisit the supernova constraints on three well-motivated light gauge bosons: the dark photon, the $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge boson, and the $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ gauge boson. For the dark photon and the $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge boson, we re-evaluate the nucleon bremsstrahlung process within the one-pion exchange approximation, retaining the full momentum and mass dependence. The geometrical dependence of the decay and absorption of these gauge bosons inside the supernova core is also taken into account. Updated bounds on these models are derived based on the cooling of SN1987A and energy deposition constraints from low-energy supernovae (LESNe). Taking the SFHo-18.8 $18.8\,M_\odot$ profile, the SN1987A cooling constraints reach masses of about $230$ MeV, $280$ MeV, and $300$ MeV for the dark photon, the $U(1)_{B-L}$ boson, and the $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ boson, while the corresponding LESN limits extend to about $450$ MeV, $440$ MeV, and $600$ MeV, respectively. The kinetic mixing parameter $\epsilon$ for dark photon, the gauge coupling $g_{BL}$ in the $U(1)_{B-L}$ model, and the gauge coupling $g_{\mu\tau}$ for the $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ model are constrained down to $5.8\times10^{-12}$, $2.9\times10^{-16}$, and $6.4\times10^{-12}$, respectively.

papers.title: Nuclear fission: from fundamentals to frontiers
papers.abstract: Nuclear fission, the division of a heavy atomic nucleus into lighter fragments, is a process of fundamental importance to nuclear physics, energy production, and the origin of the elements. This chapter, part of the Encyclopedia of Nuclear Physics, provides a pedagogical introduction to a broad array of topics in fission physics, progressing from the macroscopic liquid-drop model and microscopic shell corrections through fission dynamics, observables, modern theoretical frameworks, and experimental techniques ranging from traditional double-energy methods to inverse kinematics at radioactive-ion-beam facilities. The roles of fission in astrophysical nucleosynthesis, nuclear energy, medical isotope production, and national security are discussed, and open questions including the predictive power of microscopic theory and the fission properties of neutron-rich nuclei relevant to heavy element nucleosynthesis are highlighted.

papers.title: A living catalog of stream interaction regions in the Parker Solar Probe era
papers.abstract: Stream interaction regions (SIRs) and corotating interaction regions (CIRs) are important phenomena in heliospheric physics. These large-scale structures vary temporally and spatially, both in latitude and with radial distance. The additions of Parker Solar Probe (PSP) and Solar Orbiter have allowed for investigations into the radial evolution of these structures over a wide range of heliocentric distances for the first time since the Helios era. To better enable investigations of SIRs and CIRs within the inner heliosphere, we have developed a living catalog of SIR and CIR observations by Parker Solar Probe with corresponding observations by STEREO-A as well as ACE and Wind at 1 au. The methodology used for the identification of events and the generation of this catalog, the initial catalog of PSP observations spanning orbits one through five along with corresponding 1 au observations, and information on accessing the living catalog for future studies is described. This list of SIR and CIR events from PSP and corresponding observations from other heliophysics missions will enable case studies utilizing unique orbital arrangements, as well as aid in future statistical studies to further understand the properties and evolution of these structures.

papers.title: Delayed maximum energy solar energetic particle events: Statistical analysis from Solar Orbiter
papers.abstract: Investigations of solar energetic particles (SEPs) have long utilized the dispersive nature of onset times, as in, the earlier arrival of higher-energy particles compared to lower-energy particles, to infer information such as the path length to the acceleration site at the time of initial particle release. However, recent observations by Solar Orbiter and Parker Solar Probe have begun to characterize SEP events with an apparent delay in arrival times of the higher energy portion of the particle distribution, above a critical energy separating the delayed particles from that of the typical velocity dispersion signature at lower energies. Features of these delayed maximum energy (DME) SEP events, sometimes referred to as "inverse velocity dispersion" events, could provide new insight into the impacts of magnetic connectivity to locations along an expanding coronal mass ejection-driven (CME-driven) shock wave, variations of acceleration along the shock surface, and transport effects in the inner heliosphere. This study focuses on the occurrence rate and characteristics of DME events observed by Solar Orbiter relative to their footpoint locations with respect to the initial flare site. These DME events show a bias in occurrence rate towards events when the observer's footpoints were westward of the associated flare location. Additionally, estimated locations at which the highest-energy particles of DME events are released into the flux tube suggest continued release of increasingly higher-energy particles from the CME-driven shock into the connected flux tube well into the inner heliosphere. This indicates that DME events could be attributed to inner heliospheric effects and are not actually coronal in origin. This finding is consistent with previous observations and interpretations of SEP events connected westward of the associated flare.

papers.title: The Impact of Flyby Interactions on the Rotation of Open Clusters
papers.abstract: The Gaia astrometric mission has provided the first evidence for the bulk rotation of open clusters. While this rotation may arise from residual spin inherited from a cluster's parent molecular cloud, it is unclear whether this explanation always suffices, as angular momentum is carried away by escaping stars on the timescale of two-body relaxation. In particular, the recent observance of significant rotation ($v_{\rm rot} = 0.81 \pm 0.06$ km s$^{-1}$) in the dynamically old ($\approx 4$ Gyr) open cluster M67 motivates a study of another potential source of spin for Solar neighborhood clusters: tidal torquing from gravitational encounters with passing giant molecular clouds (GMCs). We derive an analytic estimate for the change in angular momentum of a cluster due to an impulsive interaction with a passing GMC, and verify this expectation by performing $N$-body simulations over a range of encounter parameters using REBOUND. For highly energetic encounters, significant angular momentum can be transferred, but the stars that receive the most angular momentum are ejected, leaving the cluster remnant with negligible net rotation. Even when considering a random walk of many GMC-cluster encounters, the integrated effects of these interactions cannot explain observations of dynamically old rotating open clusters. However, we find that within $\sim 5$ Myr post-encounter, some disrupted clusters could be confused as rotating clusters while their stars are still dispersing. Using the local density of GMCs, we estimate that up to $\approx 1\%$ of open clusters in the Milky Way may carry this faux-rotation signal.

papers.title: Direct measurement of the ${}^{23}\mathrm{Mg}(p, {\gamma}){}^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ reaction using the DRAGON recoil separator and a hybrid array of ${\gamma}$-ray detectors
papers.abstract: Background: The $^{23}$Mg$(p,\gamma)^{24}$Al reaction plays a key role in nova nucleosynthesis, serving as a bridge between the Ne-Na and Mg-Al cycles and impacting synthesis of a wide variety of nuclides. It is crucial that the rate of this reaction be well constrained by experimental data, in particular the properties of the key resonance at $E_{\mathrm{cm}}\approx480$ keV, which dominates the rate at nova temperatures. Purpose: Our study aims to improve experimental constraints on the energy and strength of the key $E_{\mathrm{cm}}\approx480$ keV $^{23}$Mg$(p,\gamma)^{24}$Al resonance through a new direct measurement of its strength and energy. Methods: We used a $^{23}\mathrm{Mg}$ radioactive beam to directly observe capture into the $E_{\mathrm{cm}}\approx480$ keV resonance in inverse kinematics. The $^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ recoils were selected by the DRAGON recoil separator, and coincident $\gamma$ rays were measured in a hybrid $\mathrm{LaBr}_3/\mathrm{CeBr}_3/\mathrm{BGO}$ scintillator array. The $^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ singles yield was used to determine the resonance strength, while the time difference between the coincident $\gamma$ rays and the incident beam was used to determine the resonance energy. Results: We obtained a strength of $\omega\gamma=38(7)$ meV and an energy of $E_{\mathrm{cm}}=478.8(26)$ keV for the key astrophysical $^{23}\mathrm{Mg}(p,\gamma)^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ resonance. Conclusions: Our reported strength is in excellent agreement with the previously reported direct measurement, as well as shell model calculations. Our energy is in good agreement with earlier indirect measurements. Reaction rate calculations incorporating our results indicate that the $^{23}\mathrm{Mg}(p,\gamma)^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ rate is constrained to a $1\sigma$ up/down factor of 1.5 or smaller in the nova temperature range of 0.2--0.4 GK.

papers.title: Distilling neural networks into equations to predict planetary instability
papers.abstract: The problem of predicting when a multi-planet system will become dynamically unstable has defied analytical progress over the past three hundred years. Recent machine learning advances achieve high predictive performance of instability dynamics, but as black-box systems cannot be interpreted to connect to existing scientific understanding. Here we show analytic equations that predict when a multi-planet system will undergo instability. We discover these equations by first training a neural network on a dataset of N-body simulations, and then distilling its latent knowledge into closed-form algebraic expressions. Our two-stage pipeline first learns an interpretable variable basis, then searches for equations using symbolic regression. The resulting equations outperform existing analytic estimates of instability and apply across wide ranges of mass ratios, spacing, and orbital eccentricities. They capture structure in the prediction landscape with a small number of variables amenable to dynamical interpretation. These results demonstrate how symbolic learning can be combined with neural networks to extract scientific insight from complex dynamical systems.
